coach_says: White was threatening Qxg6 mate: the queen checks on the g6-e8 diagonal, the Nc6 covers d8 and e7, and your own pieces block d7 and f8. Nb8 doesn't stop it, so after Qxg6+ your king is hunted down and mated. Rf1 was the only defence: the rook comes back so it can block on f7 after Qxg6+. When your king is this exposed, ask 'what is their checking move?' before anything else.
also: bring pieces back to defend the king

coach_says: With a pawn on c7 against a queen, and the enemy king far away, this is a draw if your king hides in the corner. After Ka8, if Black ever takes the pawn with the queen it is stalemate, and otherwise you threaten to queen. Kc6 leaves the corner, so Qd5+ drives your king away and the queen gets in front of the pawn on c8, then the black king walks over and wins it. In queen-against-pawn endings with a bishop's or rook's pawn, look for the stalemate corner.
also: queen versus pawn on the seventh

coach_says: Black's knight on e5 is pinned to the king on f6 by your queen on d4, so it can't run. Bxe5+ cashes in the pin at once, but the rook recaptures with check and joins the attack on your king. Nf3 brings your last piece into play and puts a third attacker on the pinned knight, which only the rook and king defend, so you win it next move. When a piece is pinned, pile more attackers on it instead of trading straight away.
concept: pile up on the pinned knight

coach_says: After ...f5 Black wants to play ...f4, gaining kingside space for an attack. Ng3 puts your knight right where that pawn hits it, so ...f4 comes with tempo and the knight has to go back to e2. exf5 removes the f-pawn lever before it can advance, and after ...Bxf5 Qb3 hits the loose b7 pawn. Before you put a piece somewhere, check whether an enemy pawn can kick it.
also: take on f5 to stop the kingside pawn storm

coach_says: Your knight on c3 was attacked by the rook on f3 and nothing defended it. dxc4 ignores that, so Rxc3 just wins the knight. Nxe2+ first trades it for the bishop with check, and only then do you take on c4. When one of your pieces is attacked and can't be saved, make it take something on the way out, ideally with check.

Your bishop on c2 and White's knight on d5 were both hanging. Instead of saving your bishop with Be4, take their knight first with Qxd5: if White takes on c2, Qxg2 wins a pawn, hits the h1 rook and leaves White's king stuck in the centre. Be4 just lets the knight escape to e3 and the extra material is gone. When both sides have a piece hanging, ask whether you can take theirs first.
also: recapture with the queen to hit g2

coach_says: Qh4+ looks scary, but g3 kicks the queen and it has to go home again, so you have lost two moves while White develops. It also does nothing about White's e5 pawn cramping you. dxe5 strikes at the centre right away and opens lines for your pieces. Only bring the queen out early when the check actually wins something.

Your bishop on d6 already aims at h2, and White has no knight on f3 to guard the kingside. Ng4 adds a second attacker and threatens ...Qh4 with mate on h2, so White must weaken himself, and after g3 the sacrifice ...Nxh2 Kxh2 Qh4+ picks up the bishop on c4. a5 is a slow queenside move that lets White play Nd2 and Nf3 to cover h2. When your pieces point at the enemy king and its defenders are missing, bring more pieces there.

Bxb7 starts a big trade-off where you end up only a pawn ahead in a quieter position. Bc5 saves the attacked bishop and controls e7 and f8, so Black can't develop the kingside or castle there. If Black grabs ...Nxa1, that knight is stuck in the corner and Bxb7 comes with even more force. When the opponent's king is stuck in the centre, keep your pieces and keep it stuck.
concept: keep the king stuck in the centre

coach_says: Nxg5 gives a whole knight for two pawns, and Black's king is not exposed enough for that to pay off, so you are simply down material. Your bishop on h4 was attacked, but you had a good in-between move: c5 hits the bishop on d6, and if ...gxh4 then cxd6 wins the piece back. Before sacrificing, check that you get an attack or more than two pawns, and look for a counter-attacking move first.

White's doubled pawn on g3 is a target, and your knight on c6 is not doing much against the pin from Bb5. Ne7 sidesteps the Bxc6 trade and heads for f5, where it attacks g3 together with your knight on h5. Bd7 lets White play Ne5, trade on c6 and damage your pawns. Look for the enemy's weak pawn and route your pieces towards it.
concept: reroute the knight to hit g3

coach_says: Your queen was attacked by Bg3, and Qe6 puts it in front of your e-pawn, which blocks your bishop on f8 too. It also takes the queen off the defence of c7, so Bxc7 just wins a pawn. Qd8 looks passive, but it keeps c7 covered and lets you play ...e6 and develop normally. When you retreat the queen, don't park it on a square your pawns and pieces need.

The e4 pawn was the point to strike at: your rook on e8 and knight on c5 both pressed it. Nxe4 Nxe4 exf4 attacks the bishop on e3 and opens the e-file onto the knight on e4, so you win material back with interest. Nf6 retreats, and then Bxc5 removes your good knight and f5 starts an attack on your king. When your pieces are lined up on a pawn, look for a capture followed by a pawn move that hits two things.
concept: missed Nxe4 tactic on the e-file

coach_says: With a rook against a bishop you need a passed pawn to win, and Black's h4 pawn is freezing your g2 and h3 pawns. g4 fixes that at once: if ...hxg3 en passant, h4 gives you a passed h-pawn, and if Black doesn't take, g5 runs. Kf2 is too slow, and Black's king and pawns get rolling on the queenside. In endgames, ask how you are going to make a passed pawn.
concept: create a passed pawn with g4

coach_says: The pawn on e4 was attacked by your queen and nothing defended it, so Qxe4 just wins a pawn. Bg3 gives Black time for ...Qf5, which defends e4 and offers a queen trade. Before making a quiet move, check whether any enemy pawn or piece is simply hanging.
concept: missed a free pawn on e4

coach_says: White's king had just stepped to f2, and Rd2+ checks along the second rank. Wherever the king goes, your rook then takes h2 and you are two pawns up. Kg6 is a fine move in general, but it misses a free pawn. In rook endings, look for checks that let your rook reach the enemy pawns, especially on the second rank.
also: active rook on the second rank

coach_says: White's rook on c3 was loose and his king was on the open a7-g1 diagonal. Bxe5 attacks the rook, and if fxe5 then Qd4+ checks and wins the rook on c3, getting your lost piece back. fxe5 just recaptures a pawn and lets White consolidate with Nxc4 and Be3. When you are behind, look for unprotected enemy pieces and checks that hit them.

White's bishop on f3 was eyeing b7 along the long diagonal, and Bxb7 would also hit your rook on a8. Bc5 doesn't deal with that, so Bxb7 wins a pawn. O-O-O defends b7 with the king, puts your rook on the open d-file and gets your king safe in one move. Before developing, check what their last move attacks.

Your bishop on h6 and Black's on g7 were facing each other. Qg5 lets Black take first with ...Bxh6, and after Qxh6 the knight comes to f5 and kicks your queen, so you lose time. Bxg7 Kxg7 trades off Black's best defender of the dark squares on your terms, and then you can castle. When pieces face each other, think about who benefits from taking first.

Your rook on g3 had to move, but on g5 it is attacked by Black's queen on e7 and defended only by your queen along the g-file. Ng4+ blocks that file with check, so after fxg4 Qxg5 you lose the rook, and the best you have is giving up the exchange. Rg6 keeps the rook safe and attacks e6. When a piece is defended from a distance, check whether a check can cut the line.
also: rook on a square the queen attacks
